Geopolitics & Diplomacy.title: Nvidia Freezes AI Server Shipments to Four Southeast Asian Countries Amid a US Crackdown on Remote Chip Access
Geopolitics & Diplomacy.text: SummaryNvidia has ordered its manufacturing partners to halt shipments of servers equipped with advanced AI chips to four Southeast Asian nationsThe suspension aims to stop Chinese technology companies from circumventing U.S. export controls through remote data center accessThe freeze acts as a stopgap until the Trump administration finalizes stricter guidelines regarding foreign cloud-based computingIn a major disruption to the global technology supply chain, Nvidia formally ordered its manufacturing partners to stop shipping servers containing advanced AI chips to four key Southeast Asian countries. The sweeping shipment suspension directly impacts operations in Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore and Thailand. According to initial reports from the Financial Times, prominent manufacturing partners, including Dell, already contacted buyers in the affected countries to inform them that Nvidia will not allow their pending orders to ship.The sudden freeze targets a specific operational model dominating the region. Data center operators acquiring hardware to rent out concentrated computing power to other businesses represent the primary customers for these high-end servers in Southeast Asia. Critically, some of the companies paying to lease this digital infrastructure from these Southeast Asian data centers are based in China. Chinese technology companies have increasingly utilized this rental strategy to circumvent U.S. export controls on powerful Nvidia chips, securing the necessary computational muscle by partnering with data centers safely located in non-embargoed countries.This decisive supply chain halt represents a direct response to escalating federal efforts to close the remote-access loophole that keeps Chinese enterprises connected to advanced American hardware. The U.S. Commerce Department aggressively moves to restrict Chinese technology firms from remotely accessing American-made chips through proxy companies based in Southeast Asia and Brazil. Driving this regulatory shift, the Bureau of Industry and Security published an interim final rule on November 19, 2026, specifically designed to address remote access to advanced super intelligence chips and servers. By forcing a hardware freeze at the manufacturing level, the mandate effectively severs the physical supply line that makes cloud-based evasion possible while federal regulators pivot from policing physical borders to policing digital bandwidth.The financial implications of the suspension are massive for the silicon giant, as the Southeast Asian region has been exceptionally lucrative, reportedly generating around $104 billion for Nvidia in 2025 alone. According to the New York Times, it remains unclear exactly how long the shipment suspension will last across the four nations. However, a source with knowledge of the freeze stated that the halt operates strictly as a temporary stopgap measure until the Trump administration clearly defines and implements concrete guidelines for future sales.Click here to view full gallery at Hypebeast

Entertainment.title: Innioasis Launches the Y2, a $79.99 USD Music Player That Brings Back iPod-Style Scrolling
Entertainment.text: SummaryThe Innioasis Y2 Music Player revives classic tactile navigation with an iPod-style touch-sensitive scroll ringThe offline-only device skips streaming apps in favor of user-loaded MP3s, lossless FLAC files and audiobooksHardware features include a small color screen, expandable microSD storage and both wired and Bluetooth headphone supportThe digital audio landscape is taking a calculated step backward as offline listening stages a cultural return, and the newly introduced Innioasis Y2 Music Player stands at the forefront of this shift. Arriving as a direct successor to the brand’s previous Y1 player, the dedicated digital audio player utilizes an iPod-style touch-sensitive scroll ring to navigate its menus. The release taps into a growing hardware niche for distraction-free, offline audio devices that deliberately revive the classic tactile interfaces popularized throughout the mid-2000s. Measuring just four inches tall and less than half an inch thick, the compact hardware centers its design around a small color screen positioned directly above the touch-sensitive ring, offering a customizable interface that allows users to change the display theme.Rather than relying on moving parts, the navigation wheel does not physically spin. Users simply slide their thumb around the surface to scroll through lists, ultimately pressing the center of the ring to make a selection. The outer edges of the touch ring act as controls for going back, skipping tracks and pausing playback. To streamline the listening experience, dedicated volume buttons are located entirely on the side of the device.Rejecting the modern always-on ecosystem, the device strictly plays user-loaded files and does not run streaming apps like Spotify, Apple Music or Audible. Owners must build their libraries manually, utilizing an integrated USB-C port for transferring media files from a computer. For listeners with massive archives, a microSD slot is built into the device for expanding the storage library. The system supports MP3s as well as high-fidelity lossless audio formats such as FLAC, while possessing the ability to import and export M3U playlists.Beyond standard track curation, the Innioasis Y2 supports video playback and caters to literary listeners with dedicated features that can resume audiobooks from the exact point a user stopped listening. That audiobook playback also includes an adjustable speed setting for personalized pacing.Audio delivery bridges legacy and modern standards, equipping the Innioasis Y2 with a traditional headphone jack for wired earbuds alongside Bluetooth pairing for wireless headphones. Innioasis states the player delivers up to 25 hours of music playback at half volume when using wired earbuds, though the device's specification table cites up to 35 hours of lab playback. The offline audio player is listed at a $79.99 sale price on the Innioasis US store.Click here to view full gallery at Hypebeast

Entertainment.title: Jyodan and Amiide on Turning Noriko Kose’s “Still I Miss You” Into an Award-Winning Sampling Contest Track
Entertainment.text: Noriko Kose's "Still I Miss You" — a masterpiece famously sampled in Nujabes' iconic "Reflection Eternal" and cherished globally as part of the DNA of lo-fi and jazzy hip-hop — has been breathed new life. Released in October 2025, "Still I Miss You" is a piano instrumental created by Kose as a self-homage to that very song.Using this track as their sampling source, Jyodan and Amiide took the grand prize in an official sampling contest co-hosted by Tribe (a sub-label of Hydeout Productions), SURF Music, and Hypebeast. Longtime collaborators who previously gained a core following as members of the hip-hop crew CIRRRCLE and who now operate out of Hawaii and London/Tokyo as solo artists and as the duo Otomodatchi, the pair crafted the track "but, I still miss U" out of respect for the original. While preserving Kose's beautiful piano melody, they elevated it into a new classic that bridges past, present, and future.Loved by listeners since its digital drop in January 2026, the track will see a physical 7-inch vinyl release on Sunday, December 27. To mark this milestone, Hypebeast conducted an exclusive interview with the duo. They discussed the story behind their winning track, their musical backgrounds, their current cross-border creative resonance, and their vision for the future.We wanted to convey that the story is still ongoing by inserting 'but'Hypebeast: Tell us about the production process for the winning track. How did you divide the work?Amiide (A): As soon as I heard the original track we were sampling, I made a beat and sent it to Jyodan, saying, "Try laying down some rap on this." He sent vocals back, and from there I did the arrangements and fine-tuning.How long did it take to finish?A: The total production time was about two or three weeks.Jyodan (J): I think I wrote the lyrics in a few hours. We split the recording sessions into two parts.A: Where did you get the idea for the lyrics? For this track, you added the word "but" to Noriko Kose's original title, "Still I Miss You," to create "but, I still miss you."J: Yeah, I deliberately added "but." I wanted to choose words that leave a big impact without using too many of them. That one word "but" was incredibly important. In everyone's life, there are moments when you suddenly remember a certain point in the past, right? Anytime, anywhere. By inserting "but," I wanted to create the feeling that the story is still going on right now.It's not just saying "I still miss you," but the nuance of "(time has passed since then) but, I still miss you." We sampled an updated track ("Still I Miss You") of an older song ("I Miss You") to make a modern version of it, so we wanted to express the passage of time. The environment around us changes with the times, but the feelings in our hearts remain the same as they were back then. That's the message we put into it.Listening to the tracks from your other projects (like CIRRRCLE and Otomodatchi), this one is a departure from your usual style, in a good way. I always got the impression of a positive sound reminiscent of Knxwledge or Anderson .Paak, but this time I felt a beat that somehow evoked J Dilla or Nujabes.A: I personally love Knxwledge and Anderson .Paak, but this time I decided from the start to "make a beat that shows respect to Nujabes." So instead of entering the contest under our usual Otomodatchi name, we intentionally submitted it as a Jyodan solo track (produced by Amiide).At first, I thought about singing on it too, but when Jyodan laid down his vocals, I felt it was already complete as a standalone track. I thought it would be wrong to unnecessarily add my voice to it, and that it would be better as his song. However, if the beat just stays the same, it gets monotonous, so I arranged various things on the production side so the progression wouldn't get boring.How did you feel when you first heard the vocals Jyodan sent back?A: Honestly, I was shocked because it was totally different from what I had imagined beforehand (laughs). I thought he would send back a rap that was more faithful to so-called jazzy hip-hop or lo-fi hip-hop. But the vocals he laid down were super catchy, almost reminiscent of Gym Class Heroes' "Stereo Hearts" from the 2010s. It was fresh and incredibly cool. I thought, "Ah, I would never have come up with this myself. It's the best idea born precisely because it's a collaboration."I think it's proof that the catchiness that grabs anyone's ear the moment they hear it and the respect for the original song coexist in perfect balance. As a musical challenge, it must have been a major experience for you as a producer, Amiide.A: It was really interesting. Since I don't have years of experience building a career as a producer, receiving an award like this from people like Hydeout solely based on the quality of my pure beat production — where I wasn't singing — gave me a huge confidence boost. It made me think, "It's okay for me to call myself a producer now" (laughs). This time, it's scheduled to be officially released not only digitally but also physically as a 7-inch vinyl record by Hydeout Productions. Is this the first time your audio has become physical (a record)?A: Right after the COVID pandemic started in 2020, we released a CD under our former group name, CIRRRCLE. But even though it was our first nationwide distribution and we had it stocked at Tower Records and places like that, it overlapped completely with the stay-at-home period. I have this frustrating memory of not being able to actually go and see my CD lined up in stores with my own eyes. So this time, I'm genuinely happy that the music I was involved in is becoming physical in the form of a vinyl record.The jacket artwork is also very striking. Who designed this?A: There's a senior of mine from college named Sho Hanafusa, who was a creative director at the New York culture media outlet Complex. When I casually mentioned to him, "I've got a record coming out on Nujabes' label soon," he got seriously hyped (laughs). He said, "This is historic, and I want to make it look absolutely cool, so let me do the artwork!" and ended up doing the design on short notice. この投稿をInstagramで見る Amiide アミイデ(@amiidemusic)がシェアした投稿What was the concept behind the artwork?J: It's a bit hard to explain the artwork, but I sent him some personal photos I'd taken in various countries and places I've traveled to, and had him make a collage. Like photos of food I ate on my travels that wouldn't make sense to anyone else (laughs). They're all seemingly unconnected, random photos at first glance, but to me, they're precious fragments of memory for remembering a specific woman. The lighting is distorted, the composition is slanted, but they're packed with all kinds of memories.A: When I first saw the cover art, I had no idea photos were used (laughs).J: That's fine (laughs). Everyone doesn't need to understand everything about someone else 100%. This is like a reminder to myself. How I felt, what kind of life I lived. That's locked inside the music and artwork. This project was the first time I tried not explaining the feelings and reasons inside me, even to Ami, until the production was finished. The state of being known by no one is very comfortable, and I made new discoveries.No wonder I sense a somewhat personal emotion from it.A: It's so complete as art that you can't tell it's originally a photo at first glance.Nujabes' Influence Overseas is ImmenseBy the way, from the perspective of you two who are based overseas, what is Nujabes' actual name recognition and influence like?A: Nujabes' name recognition overseas is truly amazing. He's treated as a legend, transcending the level of being famous.J: Nujabes might not be a household name everyone knows like Coca-Cola, but he's a presence that teenagers and twentysomethings sitting in a room somewhere in the world are definitely going crazy for. The parent generation might not know him, but I think anyone who is culturally aware knows him.I discovered Nujabes in college, when Shing02 came to my university to give a lecture on music and education. Through Shing02, I encountered Nujabes' music and became exposed to his work.A: I think you were trying to collaborate with Shing02 when you were in CIRRRCLE, right?J: Yeah, I was. I had a few chances to meet him after that, too. Shing02 is a really smart guy who has a master's degree in music device design and holds patents. So, being involved in a project like this, I felt a strong pressure that I absolutely couldn't write anything half-hearted.A: Come to think of it, there's a world-famous YouTuber and lo-fi music producer named L.Dre. When he was in Japan on vacation, he posted a photo on his Instagram story going to "the ramen shop run by Nujabes' brother" (*Usagi, run by Nujabes' younger brother). The place is almost a site of pilgrimage among overseas producers and fans; Nujabes' presence commands overwhelming respect.J: For the anime community and the demographic that listens to lo-fi hip-hop, Nujabes' music is the perfect bible. It's completely different from easily structured commercial music like mainstream pop, rap, EDM, or rock.It's a highly refined worldview, unlike rap that flaunts negative, flashy things like "money, cars, drugs" as seen in modern trap music. And yet, it deeply resonates with today's young kids who like anime. There's no other artist with such a unique fan base. He made music with records and old-school gear in an era without smartphones. He didn't make music for TikTok trends or dances. Despite that, modern youth still love Nujabes' music and understand how good it is. It's truly wonderful. Tell us about your own musical background, Jyodan.J: From the time I was 10, I studied and practiced everything in music, from piano, drums, guitar, and vocals to how to write metaphors in lyrics. I grew up listening to all kinds of music, like rock and country. My basic background is Texas or Southern-style rap. Plus church music, church soul like they sing in church, and Black soul. The blend of those is at my foundation. I love soul music.Were there any artists you liked back then?J: First was Dr. Dre. Then Lil Wayne, Ludacris, and Eminem were big for me. I was only listening to rap back then, and no rock at all.A: But you were also listening to Paramore and punk music, right?J: That was when I was 16. I was living on Yokota Air Base in Japan at the time, and I started listening to rock because of my friends. I loved playing the drums to rock songs back then. Because rock is actually played by humans. To do hip-hop, you needed expensive gear like samplers and drum machines, and it was an era when making that kind of music cost a lot of money. YouTube wasn't around yet, either.Back then, I liked bands like Paramore, Gym Class Heroes, Fall Out Boy, and Panic! At The Disco. Later on, I was surprised to learn they were all on the same indie label, Fueled by Ramen. All my favorite rock was gathered in one place. "Fun punk rock" tied to skateboard culture and singing about teen daily life suited me.That's quite different from your musicality from CIRRRCLE and Otomodatchi onwards. How did you come to have your current style?A: A big part of it was the three of us who were close friends going to an Anderson .Paak concert. We formed CIRRRCLE because we wanted to make a sound like his.I see. How did the two of you meet in the first place?A: Before starting CIRRRCLE, Jyodan was in a group called LOKYO, and I was in AYEN. I first became friends with a rapper named OneTwenty in LOKYO, and gradually we all started hanging out together.How long were you active as CIRRRCLE?A: CIRRRCLE was about three years, I think (2017–2020).J: Yeah. We broke up around the time of the pandemic after a lot happened.Now you're both based in different places, but you've continued producing together all along, right?A: Yes. Actually, Jyodan started living in LA midway through CIRRRCLE, so we were scattered even back then (laughs). I moved to London, and Jyodan moved around to various cities, but we were used to making songs online, so we kept making music together even while apart. Last year, we took a break from our Otomodatchi activities and focused on our solo stuff. During that time, I entered the m-flo "come again" remix contest. For this sampling contest too, I talked to Jyodan about it looking fun, and we decided to participate.How is the production environment for you, having moved your base from Tokyo to London?A: Since moving to London, being in a completely English environment has brought changes in language and thought, like being able to read English books deeply. For example, I had liked and listened to music like Cleo Sol before, but being able to understand the lyrics more deeply shifted my mindset from making music rather lightly to wanting to put deeper messages and my own thoughts into the lyrics. I also started producing proactively, and I feel like my resolution toward music has been heightened since coming to London. In October this year, I was able to release my mini-album Conversations, marking my 10th anniversary in music.Jyodan, you've moved from Texas to Japan and now to Hawaii. How have these environmental changes affected your music production?J: The basic production process is the same wherever I am, but the emotions born are completely different. Texas has wide spaces and comfortable studio environments, and my sister, who is a singer, is nearby, so I'm blessed with great support and can make my best work quickly. On the other hand, producing in Japan was truly exciting. My neighbor in my apartment was strict, so I had the pressure of having to concentrate and record at incredible speed to avoid complaints (laughs), but the noise and speed of the city of Tokyo, the scenery moving by on trains, buses, and taxis—all of it felt like a scene from a movie and was a treasure trove of inspiration.A: I still remember well the song "Mada Mada" you made on the train when you were in Japan.J: I wrote the lyrics for that while drunk on the train moving from Roppongi to Shinagawa (laughs). Amidst the rushing energy of Tokyo telling you "Hurry up, hurry up, don't be late!", I'd listen back to the recorded audio on the train, rush back to the studio, and fix it. That process was unbearably fun. Because every time you look at the city, there's a new discovery. You don't have those dizzying changes in Texas.And Hawaii, where I live now, is still a new place for me. I can say I'm working the longest hours of my life right now, spending time on work. More than school, music, family, or dates. So I'm currently in the process of gradually regaining my sense of music. But the climate and scenery of Hawaii, and the mindset you feel here, are supremely comfortable. How do you feel about the music scene in Hawaii?J: Hawaii has a strong image as a tourist destination and resort, but the music scene is actually very unique. The American Idol auditions are filmed here, too. What's interesting about the scene's characteristics is that they will arrange, remix, or sample songs of any genre into a Hawaiian style. I heard a K-pop song arranged in a Hawaiian style, and it was really interesting. There are many musically talented people, their piano, guitar, and drum skills are high, and they improve quickly. And everyone loves reggae.What's decisively different from major cities like Tokyo, London, and LA is that the scene isn't competitive. Rather than the ambition of "I'm going to be famous, look at me!", everyone is purely enjoying the music itself. If you ask, "Do you want to be famous?", I think half the people would answer, "I don't really care either way." Also, there aren't many studios in Hawaii. They park a pickup truck on the beach, and lovers, families, and local uncles gather, and a session begins. I think that's the speed—or rather, the style—of Hawaiian music.Everyone wants to keep the music they make as a secret treasure within the island; they want it to be completed here. Not in a selfish way, but they just love the spirit of the music itself. It contrasts with artists in Tokyo who think about "broadcasting to the world," but I really love the way that Hawaiian community exists, and as a result, I think it's an environment where real, good music will continue to be born for a long time.Finally, tell us about your respective visions for the future. Also, do the two of you want to return to Japan to make music again?J: Actually, I plan to move my base back to Tokyo in the future. The exact timing isn't clear, but I'd like to relocate by the end of this year or next year. I want to keep working hard on studying Japanese and continue my music career. I'd love to play lots of live shows, too.A: To all the Japanese labels out there, please hit up Jyodan (laughs). Entertainment.title: Ford Goes Like Hell Again With the Le Mans-Bound GT41 Hypercar
Entertainment.text: SummaryFord unveils the GT41 with a Zack Snyder film narrated by Matt Damon.Standing 41 inches tall, it pairs a 5.4-liter V8 with hybrid power.Racing starts in Qatar in March 2027 before Le Mans in June.Ford Racing has officially unveiled the Ford GT41, the all-new Hypercar spearheading its 2027 return to the top class of the FIA World Endurance Championship (WEC) and the 24 Hours of Le Mans. Making its public debut at Detroit’s Ford Field during the Thanksgiving Day clash between the Detroit Lions and Chicago Bears, the GT41 arrives 60 years after the marque’s historic 1966 1-2-3 Le Mans sweep.To celebrate the occasion, Ford tapped Zack Snyder and Matt Damon to create a cinematic anthem film. Shot in and around Los Angeles, the film tracks the GT41 being loaded into a shipping container bound across the Atlantic for Circuit de la Sarthe. Nodding to its heritage, the loading scene takes place inside the same hangar featured as the GT40 race workshop in Ford v Ferrari, with Damon, who portrayed Carroll Shelby in the film, lending his voice to narrate the next chapter of Ford’s enduring legacy.Named as a direct successor to the four-time Le Mans-winning GT40, the GT41 derives its name from standing 41 inches tall from the ground to its air intake. Beneath its blue-on-blue reveal livery, accented with hidden motifs of the American flag, a bald eagle, and Detroit’s “The Spirit of Detroit” sculpture, sits a 5.4-liter naturally aspirated Coyote-based V8 paired with a hybrid system. Its development draws directly from Ford’s Formula 1 partnership with Red Bull.Following European testing, testing shifts to the U.S. this December and January ahead of the 2027 WEC opener in Qatar next March and Le Mans in June. Entertainment.title: Rockstar Developers Detail the 'GTA VI' Features That Got Cut
Entertainment.text: SummaryRockstar North developers revealed in an interview with German outlet 'PC Games' that several planned 'GTA VI' features were scrapped during developmentTennis, cinema and theater visits, crawling, home decorating and crafting were all considered before being droppedThe reasons ranged from quality concerns to features that didn't fit the game's story or felt too passiveGrand Theft Auto VI arrived with a long list of activities across Leonida, but Rockstar has now confirmed that several more were dropped before launch. In an interview with PC Games during the review period, Rockstar North development manager Rob Nelson and design producer Scott Mitchell went through the mechanics and pastimes that were planned for Jason and Lucia and didn't make the final game.The biggest cut is tennis. The sport was a playable side activity in GTA V and was planned for its sequel, but according to the developers, Rockstar was never happy enough with how it played to ship it. Mini golf, on the other hand, made it into the final game, so Leonida still has at least one leisure sport.Movie and theater outings were removed for a different reason. A cinema visit or a night at the theater was considered as a way to fill downtime, but Rockstar decided these were too passive. In a game built around player control, sitting and watching apparently didn't give players enough to do.A third group of cuts dealt with how the two protagonists move through and live in their world. The team looked at letting Jason and Lucia crawl along the ground, decorate their homes and craft items. The developers said some of these ideas were dropped because they clashed with the story or the core gameplay loop, although the interview doesn't say which reason applied to which feature or how far each one got before it was cut.What did make it in reflects where Rockstar spent its effort. Nelson said the studio is proudest of the relationship between Lucia and Jason, and that the slower pacing of Red Dead Redemption 2 shaped the quieter, character-focused moments between missions. That focus seems to have paid off: GTA VI holds a Metascore of 99, matching The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time for the top score in the aggregator's history.Click here to view full gallery at Hypebeast

Economy & Markets.title: Apple Captures 57% of US Smartphone Shipments in Q3 2026
Economy & Markets.text: SummaryApple captured 57% of the US smartphone market in Q3 2026 despite a broader industry downturnRising memory costs squeezed competitors and heavily impacted the low-end Android segmentSamsung emerged as the only major Android brand to grow its market share during the quarterApple dominated the domestic hardware scene in the third quarter of 2026, capturing 57% of all US smartphone shipments. According to a Counterpoint Research report released on November 26, 2026, Apple grew its market share from 50% the previous year even as overall US smartphone shipments fell 9% year-over-year. The company stood as the only major smartphone maker to avoid a year-over-year decline in shipment volume during the quarter.This market share surge highlights a structural advantage for Apple when navigating component shortages and rising costs. While elevated memory costs squeezed the broader Android segment and forced competitors to raise prices, Apple kept iPhone pricing largely stable before releasing the iPhone 18 Pro lineup in September. Absorbing economic friction without passing the immediate burden onto consumers effectively weaponized Apple’s supply chain against rivals. Rising memory costs hit low-end Android smartphones particularly hard during the third quarter, turning an industry-wide supply issue into a competitive edge for the iOS ecosystem.Samsung managed to carve out a localized victory amidst the broader Android struggle. The South Korean company was the only major Android smartphone maker to increase its shipment share, gaining one percentage point to capture 25% of the US market. Samsung achieved this growth through a device portfolio that spanned both ultra-premium flagship models and the low-end Galaxy A-series. Other brands in the Android market lost ground, illustrating how brutal the third quarter was for manufacturers lacking scale to weather sudden spikes in production expenses.The market downturn also affected the telecommunications sector, with smartphone sales across the three major US carriers falling 4% year-over-year. Looking ahead, Counterpoint Research projects that memory costs will remain elevated for the foreseeable future, creating a persistent roadblock for hardware manufacturers. Consequently, US carriers are expected to be much more selective with their holiday promotions moving forward. Because of these compounding headwinds, overall smartphone sales are expected to remain weak throughout the fourth quarter during what is typically the peak season for consumer tech.Click here to view full gallery at Hypebeast

Art & Culture.text: SummaryPalace Skateboards is opening a two-story flagship in Beijing's Taikoo Li Sanlitun, designed around the brickwork of the Great WallGlass bricks, backlit green onyx and Chinese rosewood fill the space, alongside a hand-painted porcelain vase, a Tri-ferg fountain and a custom pianoA Beijing-exclusive capsule of tracksuits, hoodies and T-shirts pairs Tri-ferg graphics with Chinese zodiac motifsPalace Skateboards is opening its Beijing flagship in Taikoo Li Sanlitun, a 211.3-square-meter store that takes the Great Wall as its main reference. The design turns the landmark's repeating brick construction and sense of continuity into a series of materials and set pieces, filtered through the Tri-ferg graphics and tongue-in-cheek details Palace is known for.The building materials carry most of the Great Wall reference. Glass bricks and stone floors recreate the pattern and texture of the wall's masonry, while the plinths throughout the store are clad in green onyx marble. Because the onyx is translucent, Palace can light it from behind the brickwork so that Tri-ferg and P-shaped signage glows through the stone. Artificial Intelligence.title: This ER Doctor Became a Hospital’s First Clinical AI Engineer
Artificial Intelligence.text: When Boston Children’s Hospital posted a job listing for a prompt engineer in 2023, Dinesh Rai decided to apply. He didn’t expect to get the job.At the time, prompt engineering was being touted as one of the hot new jobs created by generative AI. Companies wanted people who knew how to coax the best answers from large language models (LLMs) by carefully wording instructions, supplying examples, and giving the systems personas or other context.Dinesh RaiEmployer: Boston Children’s HospitalOccupation: Clinical AI EngineerEducation: Bachelor’s degree in supply-chain management and marketing sciences, Rutgers Business School; Doctor of Medicine, Albert Einstein College of MedicineIt was an unusual role for a hospital, but Rai had an unusual résumé. While he was trained as an emergency physician, he had also taught himself to code just before entering medical school. After completing a fellowship in clinical informatics—which focuses on the intersection of clinical practice and IT systems—he moved into health technology. Boston Children’s brought him on board in August 2023. Three years later, Rai still works there. Prompt engineering, however, has become a much less important part of the job.When he joined, the expectation was that prompting would become a job in itself. “Knowing how to prompt AI properly was going to be the job function of the future,” says John Brownstein, chief innovation officer at Boston Children’s.Early on, the hospital needed internal expertise about how to begin using AI, Brownstein says. Now, better models have made elaborate prompting less important, so the harder work is building AI into actual health care systems—and determining whether its answers can be trusted. Brownstein says the questions they focus on these days have shifted: “How do you embed these tools in your day-to-day operations? How do you build agents to manage literally everything that you do?”For Rai, that has meant embracing a job broader than the role that brought him to Boston. “I’m more like a clinical AI engineer now,” he says.Between medicine and engineeringRai originally studied business as an undergraduate and began teaching himself to code in 2014 (the same year he entered medical school), as neural networks and image recognition were starting to attract wider attention. He kept building software while training as a doctor. In medical school, for instance, he created a platform called Academius for students to track residency interviews and assemble their rank lists.For Rai, the appeal of coding was its scale. In emergency medicine, he could make a direct difference for the individual patient in front of him. Software offered the possibility of building something that thousands of clinicians might use for many more patients.His 2021–22 informatics fellowship made the possibility of doing that full-time feel real. In 2022, Rai took a job at Pieces, a health care AI company, where he led work to bring LLM-based medical summarization into clinical use.That meant taking a break from practicing medicine altogether. “Stepping away was definitely a hard decision,” Rai says. But he wanted to give the technology work his full attention. He has since reactivated his medical license and hopes to return to clinical practice in some capacity within the next year.At Boston Children’s, roughly half his day now looks like an engineer’s: working with developers, writing code, and advancing projects from the technical side. The other half is spent with clinicians, figuring out what they actually need. That combination has become the point of the job. Uncovering “clinical doppelgangers”One project, called clinical doppelgangers, is designed to help doctors treating complicated patients find similar cases buried in the hospital’s historical data. Medical guidelines are generally based on large populations, but at a hospital that handles rare and complex diseases, an individual child may not fit neatly into the populations represented in published studies.The system is being developed to let clinicians identify previous patients with relevant similarities, examine their trajectories, and see how different interventions turned out. It is not meant to replace randomized clinical trials. Instead, it could provide another source of evidence when a physician is facing a case for which the published literature offers little guidance.Projects like that require more than knowing how to ask an LLM the right question. They require understanding what hospital data means, how a clinician will use an answer, and how an AI system can go wrong.Rai recently encountered some of those challenges while working on another project with a clinical team and a development team. They were deciding how much of a patient’s medical record to give an AI model when asking it to identify findings relevant to a particular clinical outcome.Better models have made elaborate prompting less important, so the harder work is building AI into actual health care systems.Both groups initially favored giving the model access to more information, but for different reasons. The developers assumed any data point could be useful. The clinicians assumed the model would recognize irrelevant findings and ignore them.Rai saw a problem with both assumptions. Clinically, an abnormal lab result or vital sign is not necessarily relevant to the question being asked. And from a technical perspective, an LLM cannot be counted on to recognize that irrelevance. If the system asks the model whether a given abnormality matters, it may construct a plausible explanation for why it does, even when the record does not support the connection.“That’s where the dual perspective has been valuable,” Rai says, “not just translating between teams, but recognizing when an approach that looks reasonable from either perspective rests on assumptions we shouldn’t make.”After the promptIn medicine, the challenges surrounding the prompt are now more important than polishing the prompt itself. Is the model’s output consistent with the underlying data? How should its results be evaluated? Will the clinician using it be able to recognize a mistake?That also means listening to clinicians’ experience. For the platform Rai’s team built to draft clinical notes, the clinicians who would go on to use the tool reviewed a batch of generated notes before anything was finalized. Someone who had cared for a complicated patient in the cardiac intensive care unit for weeks would catch an error far more easily than someone skimming the chart afterward, Rai says.Although AI adoption in medicine is surging, some health care professionals still have concerns about its use. “I think some skepticism is healthy, and we don’t try to talk people out of it,” he says. The team told clinicians up front that it was a generative AI tool meant to support their judgment, not replace their own review of the chart. “People trust it more when they’ve seen its mistakes than when we just tell them it’s good.”An evolving careerThe evolution of Rai’s role reflects how quickly AI-focused jobs can change, so Rai is wary of telling people interested in careers like his to master any particular tool. For people who want hands-on engineering jobs, fundamental programming skills still matter. Some understanding of machine learning is useful, as is experience building and testing systems. But not every clinician who wants to work with AI needs to become a database architect or take a deep dive into algorithms.What Rai considers indispensable is domain knowledge. In the medical field, that means understanding how health care workflows operate, how electronic health record data is created, what that data actually represents, and where care breaks down.That may be the more durable lesson from a career that briefly carried one of AI’s buzziest job titles. “The value isn’t just knowing how to get an answer from a model,” Rai says. “It’s knowing what context it needs and whether that context supports the answer we’re asking it to give.”
